This is by far one of the worst games I have ever played. At the time of writing this review I have 100% DS1 & 3, and Sekrio. These games were challenging with good combat and challenging game mechanics. DS2 SoFS is horrible in so many ways. I can’t think of one good thing to say about it.

The combat mechanics are the worst I have ever seen. In a game where timing and placement is key, your character is by far the slowest while the enemies feel fast and responsive. I gave up trying to parry anything! I can easily count 1 second after I press the parry button before the animation starts.This was on the same 8-bit duo wireless controller I was playing with Sekrio.
I even had an enemy turn around and strike me dead while the animation was going for the behind/backstab critical hit. My character kicked the knee of the enemy but the enemy decided to spin around and kill me instead, while I am in mid animation where I can’t block or move.
The all important i-frame is pretty much non-existent for you too. I don’t know how many times I was in mid roll and I was hit. I wasn’t in the beginning or end of the roll, I was in mid roll when it should be peak i-frame and the game doesn’t care.
More than once I was behind an enemy and tried for the backstab and only did a normal attack because I was 1/10th of a degree off from being aligned with their spine.

The hollowing mechanic just adds to the extra frustration. The more you die the more your health bar shrinks until you lose access to 50% of your health. This can make your more challenging fights all the more aggravating since you quickly go down to being killed in 1 hit and with the poor excuse of timing your character has this means you will constantly die because of these crap mechanics.

The level design is bad too, the other games gave you an idea of where to go and helped progress the story. You can wander around for a long time just to be back at where you were and have to look up on line to find some small switch in a dark corner to open a door you needed to progress through. I think I had spent over 2 hours and probably lost over 6K souls before I learned the firekeeper/level up person was DOWN THE HILL  from the main bonfire and in the shadow of a tree.

This game needlessly starts you at a disadvantage. I chose the cleric starting class and it gave me a mace as my starting weapon. Right off the bat I didn’t have to stats to weld the mace and did reduced damage. What is the point of giving me a class with a weapon if you don’t give me the stats to use it right?

Bad combat mechanics, crap response time, bad level design, doesn’t start you out right when given the option. This game is nothing but frustrating for all the wrong reasons. DS1 is older and better put together and designed than this garbage of a game.

This game is nothing but headaches and frustration, go play something else that’s actually fun.

I want to preface this by saying that I have 215.3 hours on Dark Souls III (for now), and 42.5 on Dark Souls Remastered. At some point, I do intend to go revisit DS3 with mods. All this to say, I actually did play these games and I actually do like them, unlike some people online.

To start off, the price is definitely stupid. This game used to go on sale for $10, but ever since Elden Ring came out it's been $20 with no sign of that ever changing. ♥♥♥♥ you, Bandai.

DS2 is fundamentally different from DS1 and DS3. The sheer amount of gank in this game, especially near the end, forces you to actually fight every enemy using as many tools in your arsenal as possible, as opposed to simply outrunning them and using a sword and board for the guys you want to get rid of. Some areas feel more like Halo than Dark Souls (especially because I frequently used bows to engage in ranged combat with enemies), and I actually do really like it.

An important thing to note, though, is that the game also lets you form your OWN gank squads with the sheer volume of NPC summons around to balance things out---this culminates in a triumphant conclusion to the final DLC where you bring in four allies of your own alongside two NPC summons and fight waves of enemies before the Burnt Ivory King shows up himself. And then you gank him with seven guys.

Usually, this results in a nice little balancing act. The game knows where enemies gather, and usually throws in a couple NPCs to help you with the path and the boss. For example, the optional bosses in the DLCs all have runbacks with many different enemies with clever tactical formations that make it super difficult to get around on your own, but with allies, it becomes more of a tactical free-for-all where you can actually gain control of the situation if you're smart about it. Again, this is Halo. This feels like Halo. I like Halo.

NPC questlines, such as Lucatiel's or Benhart's, also revolve around summoning them for help with bosses. It all adds up to really make DS2 feel like a shared, community experience, rather than a hopelessly isolating one like in DS1 and DS3; this fits the lore and general theme of this game.

This same idea can be seen in the hub area, Majula. In DS1 and DS3, it's a fairly dilapidated shrine with only a couple people present by the time you get there. DS2, however, has its hub in a literal village. Granted, it's somewhat of a sorry excuse for a village, but it does feel like a proper home, rather than a place for a momentary respite (or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ DS3 Firelink is, I'm not sure how to describe it). It is visibly lived in by the time you arrive, and this feeling only grows the further along you are in the game.

DS2 mostly focuses on the undead curse and the people it affects, as opposed to the linking of fire and cyclical nature of the world like in the other two games. In a sense, it's smaller than the grand quests of DS1 and DS3 (though this is very much debatable given what you learn in the latter half of the game). It's a refreshing change of pace, and I love how they integrated this into the gameplay too.

The questlines also generally make more sense than in the other two games, and are also fairly more involved. For example, the game gives you a GTA IV style dilemma unfolding throughout the game: you meet two NPCs early on in the game, with various others giving you bits of background on both of them until you eventually have to choose whose side you want to pick. You never see this kind of thing in the other two.

Now to get to the real elephant in the room: jank. While I do think DS3 is a bit cleaner, let's not pretend that DS1 isn't also a jankfest. The bosses kind of suck in DS2 (just like DS1 honestly), but the whole collaborative experience thing does make them a lot better. Off the top of my head, though, only the Pursuer and Sir Alonne were really fun on their own. DS2 hitboxes are generally pretty good, contrary to popular belief. It does seem like the grabs are stupid, but that's a result of ADP being esoteric rather than the hitboxes being *bad*, per se. Just get your agility to 99 and that's about the same as in DS3. I'd rather have ADP than a useless stat like resistance, anyway.

Overall, I'd say DS1 (Remastered) < DS2 (SOTFS) <= DS3. I have not played the original, but from what I understand, SOTFS is the "cleaner" version in terms of lore and story anyway.

游玩过程中处处都是谷村的创意和巧思，从巨人陨落之森的首尾呼应到“洛耶斯众骑士 向混沌进军！”的热血沸腾，都让我由衷佩服谷村对剧情和节奏的把控能力。dlc三部曲的几张主要地图设计更是顶级水平，这甚至让玩家间产生“DLC质量比本体高这么多，只有老贼能做这么好”于是脑补DLC是老贼回归的情况。事实上魂2的3个DLC从立项、关卡到boss设计都是古村唯操刀，盛传的老贼半路救场实际上是玩家间的谣言
魂2的本体绝大部分地图确实是小气闭塞的，但也不乏巨人陨落之森、卫龙巢穴、密港这种优秀的箱庭设计和熔铁城、堆土塔这样丰富的地图。DLC1的圣壁之都让我有魂1乌拉席露的感觉，美术设计很像法环地下的永恒之城。DLC2的黑雾之塔是魂2最优秀的地图，甚至于在整个魂系列中都是数一数二的设计。从开场的奇观、一层层探索熔炉，到点燃熔炉，借助各种升降机关重返各个楼层并探索底层。一个熔炉串联起整张地图和3个boss，DLC2的主要设计元素“火”得到了完美的呈现。DLC2的三个boss各有特点，加强后的熔铁恶魔可以被照搬到黑环，需要看滚交互的烟之骑士和充满禅意的骑士亚伦对决，三场boss战除了sb熔铁恶魔前塞个铁之回廊以外体验都很好。DLC3地图设计中等偏上，有冰冻解冻两种形态，箱庭设计不差但呈现效果一般，要是解冻的主城视觉上区别更大一点就更完美了。DLC3的最终boss战实在是难忘，召唤6个兄弟，7人合力战胜白王实在是独一份的热血体验。看到“洛耶斯众骑士 向混沌进发！”燃不起来的可以活尸化了。
总的来说，有DLC三部曲加持的魂2可谓优秀，而且越玩越像法环
